content.text: Students deepen Investigation 2 by comparing Percy’s Medusa encounter with a traditional Perseus/Medusa retelling.
Myths explain danger, power, and responsibility, and modern authors reinterpret those ideas for a new generation of readers.
This lesson prepares students for Lesson 19’s seminar, where they will synthesize ideas about heroism, power, and responsibility across myths.
Students practice comparing a modern retelling with a traditional myth and explain what that shift reveals.

Pulse Check
Which statement best explains how Riordan transforms the traditional Medusa myth?
A. Riordan removes the danger so Medusa seems harmless and misunderstood.
B. Riordan changes Percy into the villain and Medusa into the hero.
C. Riordan keeps the reflective-surface strategy but gives Medusa a voice that makes readers question responsibility and the gods’ power.
D. Riordan keeps the myth exactly the same and only updates the setting.
Part B: Writing to Compare Texts
Modeled Writing
Directions:

Use your Venn diagram notes to draft an explanatory paragraph answering this question: How does each text’s portrayal of the Medusa myth impact the reader’s understanding of Medusa? Include evidence from both texts to support your response.
Reflection

How confident are you in your ability to write an explanatory paragraph that compares ideas across two texts?

Use this routine to connect Lesson 17’s focus on Percy’s choices under pressure to today’s more complex question about whether a “monster” can also be someone who was harmed at an earlier point in their lives.

Think about your response to the question first, and then share and refine your answers with a partner.
Ask:
Why might an author retell a familiar myth from the perspective of a monster?

An author might do that so readers stop seeing the monster as only evil and start asking who had power and who got blamed. That kind of retelling can make the story feel more modern and complex because it shows that responsibility is not always simple or one-sided.

Activate prior learning from Lesson 17 and frame today’s question about how retellings can change the reader’s point of view about blame and monsters.

Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:

In this lesson, you practiced using attribution and precise pronouns to keep comparisons clear. Next, you will use these same structures to write an explanatory paragraph showing how two texts develop the same myth differently.
Support students in using attribution frames and intensive pronouns to keep comparison writing clear when explaining how two texts develop the same myth differently.
Language Focus:
Attribution frames (“In Riordan’s retelling . . . ,” “In Baldwin’s retelling . . .”)
Compare-contrast transitions (but, in contrast)
Intensive pronouns (herself, himself)
Clear noun naming to track characters across texts
Before Language Study (preparation step—optional)
Students orally compare two ideas using the frame “In ___’s retelling, ___, but in ___’s retelling, ___.”
Prompt students to name the source and character before using a pronoun.
When students use she or he, ask “Who is she? Which version?” to push for clarity.
Model how intensive pronouns add emphasis but do not replace clear naming.
You said “She blames Athena”—we can say: “In Riordan’s retelling, Medusa herself blames Athena.”
You said “He is the hero”—we can say: “In Baldwin’s retelling, Perseus is presented as the hero.”
In Riordan’s retelling, ___ herself/himself ___.
In Baldwin’s retelling, ___ is presented as ___.
In contrast, ___ ___.
Invite students to rehearse the comparison orally before writing, including in a shared home language, and then refine using attribution frames in English.
If students use unclear pronouns → Prompt: “Name the version first, then the character. Is the pronoun still clear?”
If students overuse pronouns across both texts → Prompt: “Repeat the character’s name to keep the comparison clear.”
If students misuse intensive pronouns → Prompt: “Use herself or himself only after you clearly name the person.”
Student names the source before using a pronoun.
Student uses intensive pronouns for emphasis after a clear noun.
Student explains how attribution frames make the comparison easier to follow.
Students will learn how to use attribution frames and intensive pronouns to keep comparison writing clear and precise.
Part A: Comparing Medusa Stories (RL.6.9) (12 minutes)
Students will compare Baldwin’s and Riordan’s versions of Medusa, focusing on what each keeps and what changes. This sets them up to use the Venn Diagram with a partner.
Partner Reading & Discussion
Say these Directions:

With your partner, reread the selected Baldwin excerpts and the Aunty Em scene from Chapter 11. Consider how both texts portray Medusa. On the Venn Diagram to record the details and ideas that both versions share in the middle and details and ideas that show how they differ in the outside part of the circles.
Ask:
In Baldwin’s retelling, who sets Perseus on the task, and how does that shape the reader’s first view of Medusa?

In Baldwin’s retelling, the king pushes Perseus into the task by demanding Medusa’s head. This frames Medusa as a dangerous obstacle in the hero’s mission, so readers first see her as something Perseus must defeat rather than as a character with her own perspective.
Ask:
What important myth element stays the same in both texts, and what major idea changes in Riordan’s version?

In both texts, the hero survives by using a reflective surface instead of looking at Medusa directly. However, Riordan gives Medusa a voice, which makes readers question responsibility, power, and whether Medusa is only a monster.
Pulse Check (RL.6.9)
Which statement best explains how Riordan’s Medusa compares to Baldwin’s version?
Riordan removes the danger so Medusa seems harmless and misunderstood.
Incorrect: A student might choose this if they notice Medusa’s speech but ignore that she still traps people and remains dangerous.
Riordan changes Percy into the villain and Medusa into the hero.
Incorrect: A student may choose this if they overcorrect and treat the retelling as a total reversal instead of a more complex reframing.
Riordan keeps the reflective-surface strategy but gives Medusa a voice that makes readers question responsibility and the gods’ power.
Correct: This answer captures both the preserved myth element and the changed portrayal, which is the heart of the comparison work in this lesson.
Riordan keeps the myth exactly the same and only updates the setting.
Incorrect: A student may choose this if they focus on the garden store setting but miss the important shift in portrayal and responsibility.
Support students in identifying what stays the same across both texts and explaining how Riordan changes Medusa’s portrayal to shift meaning.
Language Focus:
Across both texts
However
Unlike
This shift in portrayal suggests
Responsibility
Power

Push students beyond matching events by asking what idea each shared event supports. When students notice a difference, ask how that difference changes the reader’s view of Medusa, responsibility, or power.
You said both stories use the shield trick—we can explain that by saying, “Across both texts, the hero survives by using reflection instead of direct sight.”
You said Riordan lets Medusa talk more—we can explain that by saying, “This shift in portrayal suggests that Riordan wants readers to question who holds power and how responsibility is assigned.”
Across both texts, ___ stays the same.
Baldwin presents Medusa as ___, whereas Riordan presents her as ___.
This shift in portrayal suggests ___.

Encourage partners to talk through the comparison in everyday language first, then restate it together in academic language. Affirm that noticing unfairness, blame, or power in stories is a strong analytical move students already use in other reading.
If students list only plot details → Prompt: “Which detail changes how readers judge Medusa, not just what happens?”
If students say one version is different without naming the effect → Prompt: “How does that change affect the reader’s view of responsibility or power?”
Student identifies one shared myth element and one changed portrayal across the two texts.
Student explains how a difference shifts the reader’s thinking about responsibility or power.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Moving from Difference to Meaning

Prompt with, “Which detail changes how we judge Medusa?” and have students finish the sentence: “This matters because . . .” Organizing Comparison Evidence: Direct students to write one note in the center for what stays the same and one note on each side for what changes. Written Output: Allow students to record their comparison idea orally or use speech-to-text before turning it into writing.
Ready for extension

Add a note explaining how each version presents the gods’ power over humans. Challenge students to explain whether Riordan’s change creates more sympathy, more doubt, or both and to defend that choice with evidence.
Part B: Writing to Compare Texts (W.6.2.d) (18 minutes)

In this part of the lesson, students shift from comparing details to shaping those ideas into a clear explanatory paragraph. The modeled writing helps them see how to connect a shared myth element with Riordan’s changes, use evidence from both texts, and explain how those changes affect the reader’s view of Medusa. This prepares them to draft their own explanatory paragraph with precise language and clear attribution.
Modeled Writing
[FLAG: non-standard routine — tagging inferred]
Display the following writing model if needed for support and guidance:

In both texts, the hero defeats Medusa by using reflection instead of looking at her directly, so Riordan keeps an important part of the old myth. However, Riordan modernizes the story by changing how readers view Medusa. In Baldwin’s retelling, Medusa is mostly an obstacle in the hero’s task, and the gods help Perseus complete that mission. In Chapter 11, Medusa speaks for herself, which makes readers question who holds power and whether Medusa is only a monster. Percy still sees that she is dangerous because she tricks travelers and tries to turn people into statues. This shift in portrayal suggests that Riordan honors the traditional myth while reframing it so responsibility and power feel more complicated.
Teach: Building the Explanatory Paragraph
Say:

To build an explanatory paragraph that compares, you must first write a topic sentence that names something both versions share and something they do not. Next, choose one piece of evidence from Baldwin and one from Riordan that connect to the same big idea. Then use attribution frames so your reader always knows which version you mean. Finally, explain how Riordan’s reframing shapes the reader’s impressions of Medusa.
Say these Directions:
Use your Venn diagram notes to draft an explanatory paragraph answering this question:
How does each text’s portrayal of the Medusa myth impact the reader’s understanding of Medusa? Include evidence from both texts to support your response.
Lesson 18 Writing Rubric: Explanatory Paragraph — Riordan's Transformation of the Medusa Myth

Writing prompt: Write an explanatory paragraph explaining how Riordan transforms the Medusa myth in The Lightning Thief. Focus on the specific language choices he makes and what they reveal about how modern retellings adapt ancient myths for new audiences.
Criteria
1 — Beginning
2 — Developing
3 — Proficient
Precise Language & Style
Language Choices + Effect
The paragraph does not discuss specific language choices. General observations about the retelling are made without reference to precise word choice or its effect.
The paragraph mentions Riordan's language choices, but the analysis of what those choices reveal is vague or incomplete.

The paragraph identifies specific language choices in Riordan's retelling and explains what they reveal about how the modern version adapts the ancient myth — what is kept, what changes, and what the changes reveal about the intended audience or theme.
Gerunds & Verbals
Gerunds in Explanatory Writing
The paragraph does not use gerunds or verbals, or gerunds are used incorrectly as finite verbs.
The paragraph includes at least one gerund or verbal, but it is used awkwardly or does not add precision to a sentence.

The paragraph uses at least one gerund or verbal correctly and purposefully to add precision to a sentence about Riordan's craft or the effect of his language choices (e.g., 'By transforming Medusa into a tourist attraction, Riordan...').
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Starting the Paragraph

Offer this frame: “Across both texts, ___ stays the same, but Riordan changes ___ to show ___.” Explaining Instead of Summarizing: Prompt with, “What does this detail make the reader think about Medusa, responsibility, or power?” and have students add one sentence beginning with: “This suggests . . .” Writing Fluency: Allow students to orally rehearse the paragraph for 30 seconds and then write from that rehearsal or use speech-to-text.
Ready for extension

Add a final sentence explaining what the retelling suggests about the gods’ power. Revise one sentence to make the comparison more precise by replacing a vague word like changed with reframed, shifted, or modernized.
Reflection
Reflect on your writing ability using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in your ability to write an explanatory paragraph that compares ideas across two texts?
Support students in moving from paired details to synthesis by using academic comparison language to explain a broader idea about responsibility, power, and portrayal.
Language Focus:
Across both texts
Unlike
However
This shift in portrayal suggests
Responsibility
Power
Modernizes
Reframes

Coach students to begin with a whole-idea claim, not a plot summary. If students name a difference, push for a sentence that explains what the difference reveals about responsibility, power, or the reader’s view of Medusa.
You said “Riordan changed Medusa a lot”—we can explain that by saying, “Riordan modernizes the myth by reframing Medusa as both dangerous and more complex.”
You said “The old one is about Perseus”—we can explain that by saying, “In Baldwin’s retelling, the narrative emphasis stays on the hero’s task rather than Medusa’s perspective.”
Across both texts, ___ stays the same, but Riordan changes ___.
Unlike Baldwin’s retelling, Riordan reframes ___ by ___.
This shift in portrayal suggests that ___.

Invite students to orally rehearse the paragraph with a partner before writing so they can test the flow of their ideas. Affirm students’ ability to notice fairness and unfairness in stories as a strong resource for analyzing power and responsibility.
If students compare details accurately but stop before explaining the pattern → Prompt: “What bigger idea do these details reveal about responsibility or power?”
If students overuse vague words like different or changed → Prompt: “Can you replace that word with modernizes, reframes, or shifts the reader’s view?”
Student writes a topic sentence that names both texts and the shift in portrayal.
Student uses at least one comparison transition and one precise concept word instead of only retelling events.
Part A: Comparing Medusa Stories (RL.6.9)
Students will compare selected Baldwin and Riordan excerpts to identify what stays the same and what changes in each Medusa portrayal.
Part B: Writing to Compare Texts (W.6.2.d)
Students will draft an explanatory paragraph explaining how Riordan honors and reframes the traditional myth.
Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:
Take two minutes to look back at your draft and the question we started with. Then, turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response.
Ask:
How does each text’s portrayal of the Medusa myth impact the reader’s understanding of Medusa? Include evidence from both texts to support your response.

In Baldwin’s retelling, Medusa is mainly a monster Perseus must defeat, so the focus stays on the hero’s task. In Chapter 11, Medusa speaks for herself, which makes readers question her role and the gods’ power, even though Percy still sees her as dangerous.
Students reflect in writing on how Riordan transforms the Medusa myth.

standards.description: Use all pronouns, including intensive pronouns (e.g., myself, ourselves), correctly.
Compare and contrast texts in different forms or genres (e.g., stories and poems; historical novels and fantasy stories) in terms of their approaches to similar themes and topics.
Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.

Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

Write longer and more detailed literary and informational texts (e.g., an argument for protecting the rainforests) collaboratively (e.g., with peers) and independently using appropriate text organization and growing understanding of register.
Write short literary and informational texts (e.g., an argument for protecting the rainforests) collaboratively (e.g., with peers) and independently.
